title: Primary diffuse leptomeningeal gliomatosis as a rare cause of pain in cervical spine
case_prompt:
A 56-year-old woman with seropositive rheumatoid arthritis on long-term methotrexate presented in June 2013 with fluctuating cervical spine pain radiating to the occipital region. By early November, pain severity necessitated a 2-week hospitalization for intensive analgesic therapy. On October 27, she abruptly became noncommunicative and fixed her gaze. Examination revealed receptive and expressive aphasia and cervical paravertebral muscle tenderness without meningeal signs. Noncontrast brain CT was normal. Suspecting an acute ischemic stroke within the therapeutic window, she received intravenous thrombolysis, with rapid full recovery. Partial complex seizure was also considered. Neuropsychological testing showed mildly impaired memory and executive function. Internal, ophthalmologic, EEG, carotid/vertebral Doppler ultrasound, and CT angiography were unremarkable. She was discharged for thrombophilia screening and planned MRI.

On December 18, she was readmitted with sudden aphasia, disorientation, and a generalized tonic-clonic seizure, aborted with intravenous diazepam. She reported cervical pain, had no meningeal signs, exhibited lower-extremity hyperreflexia, and a mild paraparetic ataxic gait. MRI of the brain and spinal cord demonstrated diffuse T2/FLAIR hyperintensities in the bilateral hippocampi, brainstem, cerebellum, and spinal cord gray matter extending to T7–T8. Proton MR spectroscopy of the brainstem region showed no definite metabolic abnormalities. CSF flow studies were normal. CSF analysis revealed markedly elevated protein (12.0 g/L), albumin 4.0 g/L, mild lymphomonocytic pleocytosis (monocytes 22/µL, lymphocytes 5/µL), and a CD4:CD8 ratio of 2.94 without oligoclonal bands or red cells. Laboratory evaluation including CBC, coagulation, metabolic panel, tumor markers (CEA, CA 19-9, CA 15-3, CA 125, CYFRA 21-1, SCC antigen), hormone levels (PRL, FT4, TSH), serologies for bacterial, viral, and other pathogens (syphilis, Borrelia, Chlamydia, Mycoplasma, EBV, CMV, HSV1/2, VZV, HIV, tuberculosis, Toxoplasma, rubella), onconeural antibodies, and broad-spectrum autoantibodies were all negative. Whole-body FDG PET showed intense meningeal uptake along the cervical and thoracic spinal cord, infratentorial regions, and partially over the cerebral convexities. The working diagnosis was autoimmune meningoencephalitis with secondary epilepsy, and she received high-dose methylprednisolone (total 5 g), plasmapheresis (3 sessions), IVIG (0.4 g/kg daily for 5 days), acyclovir, and ceftriaxone.

Despite therapy, she developed a central right facial nerve palsy, left upper-limb dysmetria, spastic lower-limb paraparesis, and recurrent seizures despite carbamazepine, levetiracetam, and lamotrigine. In early February 2014, she became progressively somnolent and then semicomatose. MRI revealed hydrocephalus with enlargement of all ventricles; ophthalmologic exam showed bilateral papilledema with hemorrhages. External lumbar drainage yielded transient improvement—she remained somnolent with meningeal signs, was blind, and exhibited an organic psychosyndrome. Repeat CSF showed protein 12.9 g/L with pleocytosis (monocytes 52/µL, lymphocytes 2/µL). Interictal EEG revealed mixed slow and epileptiform activity in both temporal regions. At the end of February, MRI showed mild regression of T2/FLAIR hyperintensities, persistent hydrocephalus, and frontoparietal leptomeningeal contrast enhancement. Her condition continued to worsen with bronchopneumonia, sepsis, left subclavian vein thrombosis, and multiorgan failure. She died on April 26, 2014, approximately 10 months after symptom onset.
diagnostic_reasoning:
1. Ischemic stroke was initially suspected because “due to suspected vascular etiology with normal brain CT findings and fulfilled time window criteria, we indicated intravenous thrombolysis…”  
2. Partial complex seizure was considered since “Another possible diagnosis we considered was partial complex epileptic seizure.”  
3. Autoimmune meningoencephalitis was the leading diagnosis given the imaging and CSF profile, as “The most probable diagnosis was autoimunne meningoencephalitis with secondary epilepsy.”  
4. Infectious meningoencephalitis was investigated and excluded because “Normal findings were in the following tests: … pathogen tests (lues, borrelia, chlamydia, mycoplasma, EBV, CMV, HSV1, HSV2, VZV, HIV, TBC, toxoplasma, rubeola) …”  
5. Leptomeningeal carcinomatosis and secondary meningeal gliomatosis were considered in the differential of meningeal disease but cytologic CSF examination was not diagnostic, since “Unlike leptomeningeal carcinomatosis and secondary meningeal gliomatosis, cytologic CSF examination is usually not sensitive enough in PDLG.”  
6. Primary diffuse leptomeningeal gliomatosis was confirmed postmortem when “Despite sampling of whole brain and spinal cord tissue, no similar tumorous lesion was found. These findings match criteria for PDLG.”
